hints: For each energy type, identify the physical feature of the ball that gives it that energy.
Gravitational potential energy depends on position in a gravitational field; kinetic energy depends on motion or speed.
walkthrough: Gravitational potential energy is energy stored by a mass because of its position or height in a gravitational field.
Kinetic energy is energy an object has because it is moving, so it depends on its speed.
For the falling ball, a change in height changes its gravitational potential energy, while its increasing speed changes its kinetic energy.

ai_rubric.observable: States that gravitational potential energy is associated with a mass's position or height in a gravitational field.
States that kinetic energy is associated with an object's motion, speed or velocity.

hints: The displacement between A and B is the area under the velocity–time graph between 0.40 s and 0.80 s.
The straight-line section forms a trapezium with parallel sides 3.9 m s⁻¹ and 7.8 m s⁻¹ over 0.40 s.
walkthrough: Displacement is the area under a velocity–time graph. From A to B, the time interval is 0.80 − 0.40 = 0.40 s.
Read the velocities at the endpoints: 3.9 m s⁻¹ at A and 7.8 m s⁻¹ at B.
The area is a trapezium, so displacement = ½(3.9 + 7.8) × 0.40.
This gives 2.34 m, which is 2.3 m to two significant figures in the direction of the falling motion.

ai_rubric.observable: Chooses a valid route from the graph: trapezium area using endpoint velocities, or acceleration from its gradient followed by a constant-acceleration displacement relation.
Uses the graph readings consistently, for example ½(3.9 + 7.8) × 0.40, to determine the displacement.
Obtains a displacement of about 2.3 m.

hints: Acceleration is the gradient of the velocity–time graph between A and B.
Read the velocity increase from 3.9 m s⁻¹ to 7.8 m s⁻¹ over the 0.40 s interval.
walkthrough: On a velocity–time graph, acceleration is the gradient: a = Δv / Δt.
From A to B, velocity changes from 3.9 m s⁻¹ to 7.8 m s⁻¹ in 0.80 − 0.40 = 0.40 s.
To the graph-reading precision, the acceleration is 9.8 m s⁻² in the direction of the motion.

ai_rubric.observable: Uses the velocity–time gradient or the equivalent change-in-velocity-over-time relationship for acceleration.
Uses 7.8 m s⁻¹, 3.9 m s⁻¹ and 0.40 s to obtain an acceleration of about 9.8 m s⁻².

hints: Use the graph to read the speed at A and the speed at B, then compare the kinetic energies at those two speeds.
The change is final kinetic energy minus initial kinetic energy, using Eₖ = ½mv² with m = 1.5 kg.
Substitute 7.8 m s⁻¹ for the final speed and 3.9 m s⁻¹ for the initial speed.
walkthrough: The graph gives an initial speed of 3.9 m s⁻¹ at A and a final speed of 7.8 m s⁻¹ at B.
Use Eₖ = ½mv², so the change is ΔEₖ = ½m(v² − u²).
The kinetic energy therefore increases by 34 J.

ai_rubric.observable: Uses the kinetic-energy relationship Eₖ = ½mv².
Forms the final-minus-initial kinetic-energy change using 1.5 kg and the graph speeds 7.8 m s⁻¹ and 3.9 m s⁻¹.
Obtains an increase in kinetic energy of about 34 J.

hints: Use the displacement from A to B found in part (b)(i); the gravitational force and the ball's motion are both downward.
Calculate the weight from mg, then multiply it by the 2.3 m displacement.
Compare that work with the kinetic-energy increase from part (b)(iii).
walkthrough: The gravitational force is the ball's weight: F = mg = 1.5 × 9.8 = 14.7 N downward.
The ball moves 2.3 m downward, in the same direction as this force, so work done by gravity is W = Fs.
W = 14.7 × 2.3 = 33.8 J, which rounds to 34 J.
This matches the 34 J increase in kinetic energy found in part (b)(iii), as required.

ai_rubric.observable: Uses work done as force multiplied by displacement, with gravity's force expressed as mg or an equivalent weight value.
Calculates gravitational work as about 34 J from the 1.5 kg mass and 2.3 m displacement, and identifies that it equals the kinetic-energy increase.
